transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well... I suppose what finally got me to call is that some mornings I wake up—or I’m lying there before I’m fully up—and I think, it might just be easier if I hadn’t woken up at all. And then I scare myself a bit, because I’m not the kind of person who usually talks that way.

I don’t have some plan to hurt myself or anything like that. It’s more... that thought keeps showing up, and I thought maybe I shouldn’t just keep brushing it off.
How long have you been having these thoughts about not wanting to wake up?

About a month, I think. It started after my sister died—she died unexpectedly, and since then mornings have just been... different. I keep thinking of calling her, you know, because we had this silly habit of checking in about the weather, of all things. And then I remember. So yes, I’d say it’s been going on since then, about a month.
Have you noticed any changes in the things you normally enjoy doing since your sister passed away?

Yes… I have. I still go, you know, to book club, and there’s a dance night I’ve gone to for years—though half the time we mostly gossip by the refreshment table more than dance, if I’m honest. And I do make myself show up because I think, well, if I stop going then everyone will worry.

But lately I’m there and it feels like I’m sort of behind a pane of glass, watching everyone else enjoy themselves. Even my garden… usually I get such pleasure out of fussing over the tomatoes or cutting herbs, and cooking something for the neighbors used to give me this little lift. Now I do it, but it just doesn’t feel the same.
Have you noticed any change in your weight since your sister passed away?

I think so, yes. I haven’t been trying to lose weight, but food just doesn’t really call to me lately. I’ll make a piece of toast, or maybe a little soup, and then somehow it’s evening and I realize that’s almost all I’ve had.

It’s funny, because I used to be the one who’d insist everyone eat something—my sister used to tease me about always pushing leftovers on people. But for myself now, I just don’t seem to think about it much.
Have you been feeling slowed down or restless since your sister passed away?

I’m not sure, really. I mean, I do sit longer than I used to, but then again I’ve always been one to sit with a cup of tea and look out the window—my sister used to say I could make an afternoon disappear that way. Restless… I don’t know. I haven’t noticed pacing or anything like that. Maybe I’m just moving through the day differently, but I couldn’t say clearly one way or the other.
Have you felt hopeless about the future since your sister passed away?

I don’t know if I’d call it hopeless, exactly. That sounds so… final, doesn’t it? I do have moments where I look ahead and it feels awfully quiet, but then I’ll remember I need to water the geraniums or I promised someone I’d bring back their casserole dish.

My sister and I used to talk about silly future things—like whether we’d become the sort of old ladies who wore purple hats to lunch. I suppose when I think about that, it’s hard not to feel a bit… blank. But hopeless? I’m not sure. I don’t think I can answer that neatly.
Have you been feeling guilty about anything since your sister passed away?

Yes… I suppose I have. I keep thinking about those last weeks with her, turning it over and over, like when you misplace a recipe card and keep checking the same drawer even though you know it isn’t there.

I tell myself I should have called more often, or sat and really listened better when she was talking. Maybe I should have done something more useful instead of fussing with little things—tea, blankets, all that. Part of me knows I probably couldn’t have changed what happened, but that doesn’t seem to stop me from going back over it.
How many days in the past month have you felt this way, with thoughts of not wanting to wake up and feeling behind a pane of glass?

I… I don’t know the exact number. Not every day, I don’t think. But enough mornings that it frightened me into asking for help. I wake up and there’s this thought that maybe it would be easier if I just didn’t wake up at all.

I should say—I don’t have a plan to hurt myself. It’s not like that, exactly. It’s more like being behind a pane of glass, watching the day start without me. Some mornings it passes once I get up and put the kettle on, or notice the mail needs bringing in… but it has happened several times this past month.
How many weeks have you been feeling this way, with thoughts of not wanting to wake up and feeling disconnected from activities?

About four weeks, I think… since my sister died. It was so sudden, and I keep measuring time by all these little things—like the sympathy cards still sitting on the side table, and someone brought a lemon cake I never did finish.

But yes, to answer you properly, it’s been about a month that I’ve had those thoughts and felt so separate from things.
Have you lost interest in activities that you normally find pleasurable?

Yes… I suppose I have. I still make myself go to things, like book club, and there’s that dance night—though I mostly just sit and watch now. Last time someone was talking about a novel with a missing letter in it, and I kept thinking about how my sister would’ve said the ending was too tidy.

But, sorry… yes, the answer is yes. I’m there, but it feels like I’m behind that pane of glass again. Even my garden doesn’t give me that little lift it used to, and cooking something for the neighbors just feels like going through the motions.
Have you had at least two weeks where you felt this way nearly every day?

Yes… yes, I think so. It’s been about a month now, since my sister died so suddenly. Time’s gone strange, honestly—there are still little things of hers I keep thinking I should tell her about, and then I remember.

But yes, at least two weeks. It’s been going on most days for about a month.
Have you felt worthless since your sister passed away?

Yes… I have. Not all the time in some grand way, but I keep turning over those last weeks with her, like if I look at them enough I’ll find the place where I failed.

I tell myself I should’ve called more, or listened better when she was tired, or done something actually useful. And then I’ll remember something silly, like she’d asked me about a recipe and I never wrote it down for her—though that probably has nothing to do with anything.

Part of me knows I couldn’t have changed what happened. But it still feels like… I should have done more.
Have you been having thoughts of death or dying frequently since your sister passed away?

Yes… not like I’m making plans, no. I should say that clearly. I don’t have a plan to hurt myself.

But I have had mornings where I wake up and think… it might’ve been easier if I just hadn’t. If I’d just slept through, you know? And then I feel awful even saying that, because my sister—well, she would’ve hated hearing me talk that way. She used to call me in the mornings sometimes, always too cheerful before coffee.

But yes. That’s what frightened me enough to come here, really. Those thoughts have been coming up.
Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly or feeling like it's harder to get things done since your sister passed away?

Yes… yes, I have. It’s strange, because I’ll think, “Oh, I’ll just run one errand,” or “I’ll just get those papers together for the Cultural Center,” and then it feels like I’ve done some enormous thing.

My body feels slow, like I’m moving through thick mud. Even small tasks wear me out more than they should.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight since your sister passed away?

I don’t know if it’s a “significant” amount… I haven’t been carefully tracking it. But food just doesn’t really call to me much anymore.

I’ll make a piece of toast, or some soup, and think that’s enough for now—and then by evening I realize I’ve barely eaten. I’m not trying to lose weight. It’s just… eating feels like something I forget how to care about.
Have you felt that these thoughts of not wanting to wake up are interfering with your daily life most days?

Yes… I think they are. Not every single moment, but most days it sort of throws me off before I’ve even started.

I had to ask another volunteer to take over parts of the Juneteenth budgeting workshop, which… I hate doing that. I’m usually the one with the folders and the little color-coded notes—my sister used to tease me about that, actually, said I could organize a tornado. But I just can’t keep up with the preparation the way I normally would.

And I’ve been turning down neighbors and friends more than usual. Little invitations, stopping by, helping with things. I just… I don’t have the room in me for it lately.
Have you had any days in the past month where you didn't have these thoughts of not wanting to wake up and felt somewhat normal?

There have been… a few quieter mornings, I suppose, where I can make coffee and look out the window and almost feel like myself for a little bit. But what scared me enough to come ask for help is that I keep having these mornings where I think, “Maybe it would be easier if I just didn’t wake up.”

I don’t have a plan to hurt myself. I want to be clear about that. It’s more like the thought is just sitting there when I open my eyes. And then I think about my sister, and about how she always said the morning light in the kitchen was the best part of the house—funny what sticks with you—and I feel ashamed that I’m not appreciating it the way I used to.
Have you had any periods of at least two weeks in the past month where you felt better and your symptoms improved?

No… not really for two whole weeks. This has really only been about a month altogether, since my sister died so suddenly.

There are little stretches where I think, oh, maybe I’m doing all right today—like if I’m folding laundry or watering the plant she gave me, which I’ve nearly killed twice—but it doesn’t last. I wouldn’t say there’s been a solid period where things lifted and stayed better.
Have your symptoms been present for most of the day, nearly every day, for the past two weeks?

It’s been… about a month now, really, since my sister died so unexpectedly. I keep thinking I should be able to mark time better—she was the one who always remembered dates, birthdays, when the church supper was, all of that—but yes, this has been hanging around most days since then.
Have you experienced a depressive episode that has lasted for more than two months?

No, not more than two months. It’s been about a month… since my sister died so suddenly. I keep counting it by little things, like the grocery delivery dates and the neighbor’s roses blooming, which is probably not how normal people keep track, but—no, it hasn’t been two months.
